title: How to email your lecturer
summary: What to write, what to leave out, and copy-and-paste templates for questions, extensions and missed classes.
body:
*Sample guide. Replace this with the text from your Google Doc.*

Emailing a lecturer can feel like a big deal, but they get emails like yours every day. A short, clear email is all you need.

## Before you write

- **Check the course page first.** The answer might already be in the course outline or on Canvas.
- **Use your University email.** Emails from personal accounts can end up in spam.
- **Find the right person.** Tutors often handle tutorial questions. Course coordinators handle extensions.

## What to include

1. **A clear subject line** with the course code, like *COMPSCI 101: question about Assignment 2*
2. **A greeting**, like *Kia ora Dr Smith* or *Hi Sam*
3. **Who you are:** your name, student ID and course
4. **What you need**, in one or two sentences
5. **A sign-off**, like *Ngā mihi* or *Thanks*, and your name

## Templates

### Asking a question

> Subject: COURSE 101: question about Assignment 2
>
> Kia ora [name],
>
> I'm [your name] (ID [number]) in COURSE 101. I wasn't sure what question 3 of Assignment 2 means by "[quote]". Could you clarify what you're looking for?
>
> Ngā mihi,
> [your name]

### Asking for an extension

> Subject: COURSE 101: extension request for Assignment 2
>
> Kia ora [name],
>
> I'm [your name] (ID [number]) in COURSE 101. I'm writing to ask for an extension on Assignment 2, due [date]. [One sentence on why, if you want to share.] Would [new date] be possible?
>
> Ngā mihi,
> [your name]

You don't have to share a diagnosis or personal details. If you're registered with Student Disability Services, you can mention that instead.

## Tips

- It's fine to keep it short. Short emails get answered faster.
- No reply after three working days? A polite follow-up is completely normal.
- Feeling stuck? Bring a draft to an AUNSA study session and we'll help.

title: AUNSA resource guide
summary: Where to go at the University for study support, adjustments, health and wellbeing, explained in plain language.
body:

There's a lot of support at the University, but it can be hard to know where to start. Here's a quick map.

## I want help with studying

**Inclusive Learning** works with neurodivergent students on study strategies, and runs online hangouts where you can meet other students.

## I need adjustments for tests, exams or classes

**Student Disability Services** can talk with you about support and arrangements for tests and exams.

## I want to talk to a doctor, nurse or counsellor

**University Health and Counselling Service** is on campus for enrolled students.

## I need to talk to someone right now

Free call or text **1737** any time to reach a trained counsellor. In an emergency, call **111**.

---

You'll find links to all of these, plus national organisations, under *Useful links* on the Resources page.
